text: A list view has its own Configure option, separate from Form Layout, called List Layout. It uses the same two-column picker idea as forms, but instead of picking fields for one record, you're picking which columns appear across every row in the list, and in what left-to-right order. Add Caller as a column and every row shows that incident's caller. This only changes what's displayed — it never changes which records satisfy the list's filter or what data those records actually hold.

A table isn't limited to one list layout. ServiceNow lets you define several named views on the same table — a Default view with general-purpose columns, and a Service Desk view tuned for frontline triage, with Caller, Short description, Priority, and Assigned to. Which view a given user sees can depend on their role or their own selection from the list's view picker. That's exactly why two people looking at the same Incident list can see completely different columns: same records, different named views.

Click any column header and the list sorts by that column, ascending, then descending on a second click — the records don't change, only their order. Right-click a column header and choose Group By to cluster rows that share a value — grouping by Priority clusters all Priority 1 records together, then Priority 2, and so on, each cluster with a collapsible header. Neither sorting nor grouping removes a single record; they're purely about presentation.

Right-clicking a cell, not just a header, opens a context menu with quick actions scoped to that value or row — copying a record's URL, emailing a link, or updating a value across every selected row at once, without opening each form individually. For a Service Desk lead reassigning fifty incidents from one group to another, this context menu is often faster than opening fifty forms one at a time.

List Layout picks columns, named views let different teams see different columns on the same data, sorting and grouping reorganize without filtering, and the context menu acts directly on rows. Next up: building real filter conditions and reading the breadcrumb trail they leave behind.
